claims.text: Local lattice distortions and short-range chemical order are the primary mediators governing strength in multi-component concentrated alloys.
Local lattice distortions and short-range chemical order influence deformation and failure behavior.
The as-cast near-equiatomic alloy contains inherent local lattice distortions.
The as-cast near-equiatomic alloy contains incipient short-range chemical order.
A high-temperature annealing treatment can reduce short-range chemical order without significant grain growth or phase change.
Reducing short-range chemical order will lower the amplitude of local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions generated by multiple principal elements produce heterogeneous internal stresses.
Short-range ordered regions act as dislocation-pinning points.
Heterogeneous internal stresses and short-range ordered regions impede dislocation nucleation and glide.
Controlled annealing that reduces order will diminish local barriers to dislocation motion.
Annealed samples with reduced short-range order will have lower yield strength than the as-cast baseline.
Annealed samples with reduced short-range order will show a greater tendency toward uniform deformation than the as-cast baseline.
The as-cast alloy has higher yield strength and deformation resistance because of its lattice distortions and short-range order.
The proposed effect should remain observable below recrystallization when grain size and phase constitution are held comparable.
Significant grain growth, secondary-phase formation, high-temperature creep, or twinning at extreme strains may obscure the proposed effect.

A failure to observe a statistically significant yield-strength decrease after confirmed reductions in short-range order and lattice distortion would falsify the proposed governing-strength hypothesis.
